messages.subject: Autocorrelation and non-independence in distsamp
parts:
I would like to analyze distance sampling data from line transects using unmarked, however, I'm struggling with whether or not it will work with my data set.

My observations are chimpanzee nests along transects. Given that chimps build a new nest every night, and that the decay rate is ~5months, my data may show autocorrelation. Therefor should I add an autocorrelation term, and is this possible to incorporate into distsamp?

Additionally, my study design was set up such that multiple study sites were randomly placed across a national park. Then within each site, transects were randomly placed. As my transects are therefore contained within individual study sties, there is a question of non-independence. Should I add a random effect to account for this non-independence? If so, is there a way to do this in distsamp?
Otherwise, would it be appropriate to simply add study site as a covariate in my model to account for this?

Any advice on these two issues is greatly appreciate. And if unmarked is not the appropriate choice for carrying out my analysis given my dataset, does anyone have a suggestion on an alternative?

messages.author: 02d195331194f5bd
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Autocorrelation and non-independence in distsamp
parts:
In terms of software for analysis, you basically have 3 options: 
1) package unmarked in R
2) program Distance
3) write a custom model in your software of choice
Of those 3, if you have the statistical and programming chops to write your own model, then go for it! A custom model is the only way to add an autocorrelation term or the type of random effect you want. Autocorrelation is typically incorporated as a variance-covariance matrix on the errors/residuals of a linear model. There is a random effect in unmarked models, but it refers to the unobserved, "true" abundance at each sampling location (as opposed to the mean abundance across locations, which is the abundance estimate that the model returns in the results). A third advantage of a custom model would be to propagate uncertainty around chimp nest decay rates through the model. However, it takes a lot of knowledge and/or effort to write your own model, so if you're not going that route, I'd recommend unmarked. It fits a lot of different models and allows for easier incorporation of covariates of abundance than does program Distance. 

If you're fitting a model in unmarked, you could include site as a fixed effect. There's nothing wrong with that approach. In terms of autocorrelation, are you concerned about autocorrelation in that chimps don't nest independently, and individuals in a group will all nest near one another? People often deal with that type of autocorrelation by modeling the number of clusters/groups of individuals rather than the number of individuals (if you can easily define clusters). Or are you concerned about autocorrelation that could arise if/when chimps preferentially go back to the same area to nest, resulting in spatial correlation that forms over time? That's tricky. Do you know how other nest-based surveys deal with that issue? I guess I'd start by fitting a model in unmarked and testing for autocorrelation in the residuals. I'm curious what other folks will have to say. 

Philip Shirk

messages.author: e5841ce9d01eda50
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Autocorrelation and non-independence in distsamp
parts:
Philip,

Thank you for your reply.
Unfortunately, I definitely don't have the chops to completely make my own model, at least not at my current level. I wish!

I'll try as you suggest though and try using unmarked with site as a fixed effect, thank you for the advice on that.
And my concern is over spatial autocorrelation whereby I could be counting nests along the same transect that are from the same chimp but different days. Chimps are known to be far ranging, both daily and overall, but there is no way to know if a nest is from the same or not if the age of the nest is different. 
Am I thinking about this correctly that autocorrelation could be a concern here?

Certainly, it may be useful to run the model and test for autocorrelation afterwards.

Thanks!
Adrienne
